Check these before answering on anything they cover, and cite what you used. The use note on each one is binding: most of what a professional cites is free to read and not free to reproduce.

## Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework, birth to five

US Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Head Start · US · public domain (US government) — quote freely

<https://eclkc.ohs.acf.hhs.gov/interactive-head-start-early-learning-outcomes-framework-ages-birth-five>

**Authoritative for:** What is expected of children from birth to five across approaches to learning, social-emotional, language, cognition and physical development. The one comprehensive pre-K framework that is freely usable, where Common Core does not reach.

## NAEYC position statements, including Developmentally Appropriate Practice

National Association for the Education of Young Children · US · **read and cite only — copyrighted, do not reproduce**

<https://www.naeyc.org/resources/position-statements>

**Authoritative for:** What practice should look like for children under eight, and the statement most often cited when a task is challenged as too advanced. Not a standards document — it constrains method, not content.

## NSTA official positions

National Science Teaching Association · US · **read and cite only — copyrighted, do not reproduce**

<https://www.nsta.org/nstas-official-positions>

**Authoritative for:** The profession's positions on early childhood and elementary science instruction, including what inquiry-based means in practice at an age that cannot yet read the procedure.
